clue.text: It's* a vital matter

parts.note: vital in the sense of living: the clue describes the living substance of cells, with matter read as stuff rather than an issue

explanation.surface: Someone stresses that an issue is of great importance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vital matter' reads as an important issue; in fact vital means of life and matter means substance.
explanation.definitionFit: The jelly-like living material inside every cell is literally the matter of life.

clue.text: -In truth, the friend of the sappers

parts.note: the Royal Engineers, the army corps of sappers, are RE
an ally is a friend or supporter

explanation.surface: Someone claims honestly to be on the side of the army's engineers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of' is a link: the friend of RE is RE's ally.
explanation.definitionFit: Truly, or as a matter of fact, is what this adverb means.

clue.text: As well to be this in the driver's place on the whole

parts.note: a golfer hits a drive from the tee, so the tee is where the driver stands
the whole amount is the total

explanation.surface: Advice that a motorist would be wise to avoid drink entirely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Driver' suggests a motorist, which fits the definition's advice, but in the wordplay it is a golfer's driving club, played from the TEE. 'on the' joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue's definition is a sentence frame: a motorist is wise to abstain from alcohol, the state of someone who never drinks.

clue.text: A paradox among instruments

parts.note: the Italian name of this keyboard means soft-loud, a contradiction in terms

explanation.surface: Some musical device seems self-contradictory.
explanation.walkthrough: The instrument's full Italian name joins piano, soft, and forte, loud.
explanation.definitionFit: The full name of the piano combines two opposite dynamic markings.

clue.text: Naval instances of a girl in arms .

indicators.note: the girl is placed in the weapons, one word inside the other

parts.note: Ada is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A young woman bearing weapons is an example of sea power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of a' is link wording; the Spanish Armada is the famous fleet.
explanation.definitionFit: Great fleets of warships are cases of maritime force.

clue.text: Courses-taken in or out of school

definitions.text: Courses-taken in or out of school

parts.words: Courses-taken in or out of school
parts.note: courses read as dishes served at the table, eaten at school or at home, not classes

explanation.surface: Lessons can be studied in class or elsewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Courses' suggests study but means dishes of food, as served at school dinners or home.
explanation.definitionFit: A lunch or dinner is a set of dishes, eaten anywhere.

clue.text: Devise nice plan for getting — to the top

indicators.note: to devise is to work out anew, so the letters are re-formed

explanation.surface: Someone plots a clever scheme to rise to the summit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for getting to the' is link wording.
explanation.definitionFit: A peak or summit is the highest point.

clue.text: Small establishment organizes teas on time

indicators.note: to organize is to arrange, so these letters are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A little business lays on tea punctually.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Establishment' suggests a business; it is a small residence.
explanation.definitionFit: A self-contained flat over two floors is a modest home or household.

clue.text: Girl sees another round Mayfair

indicators.note: one girl's name is placed round the postcode, enclosing it

parts.note: another girl, here the name Edna
Mayfair is in London's W1 postal district, written here as WI

explanation.surface: One woman visits another in an upmarket part of London.
explanation.walkthrough: W1 is the London postcode covering Mayfair, with the figure 1 treated as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: Edwina is a female first name.

clue.text: But not a handy calendar for a fruit-supplier

definitions.text: But not a handy calendar for a fruit-supplier

parts.words: But not a handy calendar for a fruit-supplier
parts.note: a calendar held in the hand would be a diary in the palm; the clue says it is instead the tree that bears the sweet fruit

explanation.surface: A grocer is told that something is no pocket diary.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke splits the answer into a calendar day and the palm of the hand, then rejects that reading for the tree.
explanation.definitionFit: This tree of desert oases yields the sticky brown fruit eaten dried.

clue.text: Workers swallow lime concoction — to cure them ?

indicators.note: the insects take the mixed letters into themselves, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: worker ants are the classic crossword workers

indicators.note: a concoction is a mixture, so the letters of the citrus word are mixed up

explanation.surface: Labourers drink a lime brew as a remedy for their illnesses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'them' stands for the answer: the clue pictures a lime remedy for illness, as lime juice once cured sailors of scurvy.
explanation.definitionFit: The pronoun stands for complaints of the body, the illnesses a remedy treats.

clue.text: Sort of Tory peasant

indicators.note: to sort something is to put it in a new order, so the party word is rearranged

explanation.surface: A Conservative is described as a kind of rustic.
explanation.walkthrough: A ryot is an Indian peasant farmer, a word from the Raj.
explanation.definitionFit: In India a ryot was a tenant cultivator, a smallholding farm labourer.

clue.text: Disreputable fellow's horseplay with a cake

parts.note: a rag is a boisterous student prank
a muffin is a small cake

explanation.surface: A rogue is described as rowdy fun with something baked.
explanation.walkthrough: 's is short for 'is', linking definition and wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A ragged, scruffy urchin is a disreputably dressed person.

clue.text: Bacon container is in order .

parts.note: Francis Bacon, the Elizabethan philosopher and statesman
a can is a tin container

explanation.surface: A tin for rashers is kept tidy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bacon' looks like breakfast but is Francis Bacon; a different Bacon, the friar Roger, was himself one of these. 'is' links: the friar is one in a religious order.
explanation.definitionFit: A friar of the order founded by St Francis of Assisi belongs to a religious order.

clue.text: Evidence of devilry afoot

parts.note: afoot read literally as on the foot: the Devil's split hoof is the sign

explanation.surface: Signs suggest wickedness is going on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Afoot' means under way but also on a foot, where Satan's split hoof shows.
explanation.definitionFit: The Devil is traditionally pictured with a split hoof like a goat's, the mark of Satan.

clue.text: Their charges are restricted by law

definitions.text: Their charges are restricted by law

parts.words: Their charges are restricted by law
parts.note: charges read as people in someone's care, here prisoners locked up under the law, rather than fees capped by legislation

explanation.surface: Some professionals' fees are capped by regulation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charges' suggests prices limited by statute; the people in charge are prison warders, whose charges are inmates confined lawfully.
explanation.definitionFit: Prison warders keep custody of inmates confined under a court's sentence.

clue.text: .Protests against refusal of an appeal

definitions.text: Protests against refusal of an appeal

parts.words: Protests against refusal of an appeal
parts.note: loud complaints when an appeal is turned down, punning on cricket fielders shouting their appeal for a dismissal

explanation.surface: People object when their legal appeal is rejected.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket fielders appeal by shouting for a dismissal; if the umpire refuses, the cries were in vain.
explanation.definitionFit: Public clamours of objection are loud protests.

clue.text: Fine for Smith, it appears

parts.note: F. E. Smith, Lord Birkenhead, the British lawyer and politician, known by his initials

explanation.surface: A man called Smith seems to have been charged a penalty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smith' suggests a blacksmith, or iron's symbol Fe; it is F. E. Smith, the Conservative Lord Chancellor of the 1920s. 'appears' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A penalty paid for wrongdoing is something given up, like a monetary penalty.

clue.text: Alice got the bird, and put it to striking use

definitions.text: Alice got the bird, and put it to striking use

parts.words: Alice got the bird, and put it to striking use
parts.note: in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland the croquet mallets are live pink wading birds

explanation.surface: A girl was booed and hit back hard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Got the bird' suggests being jeered; in Lewis Carroll's story Alice is handed a bird as a croquet mallet.
explanation.definitionFit: Lewis Carroll's Queen of Hearts' croquet uses pink wading birds as mallets.

clue.text: As one is said to be, while still alive

definitions.text: As one is said to be, while still alive

parts.words: As one is said to be, while still alive
parts.note: the proverb says that while there is life there is hope

explanation.surface: Something is said of the living.
explanation.walkthrough: It turns on the proverb 'while there's life there's hope'.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb links life with optimism, so the living are optimistic.

clue.text: Fiery enough to seem to melt perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the words are only one possible arrangement of these letters

explanation.surface: Something is hot enough that it looks ready to liquefy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'enough to' is link padding; the anagram uses SEEM TO MELT, the second 'to' of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A spirited, high-mettled horse or person is full of fire and courage.

clue.text: Sailor-to-be taking orders

parts.note: AB, able-bodied seaman, is the usual crossword sailor

explanation.surface: A future seaman is obeying commands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking orders' sounds like obeying a superior; here it means entering holy orders, as a French cleric has done.
explanation.definitionFit: A French abbé is a priest, someone who has entered holy orders.

clue.text: A little quarrel blowing up

definitions.meaning: a dated word for a minor row

explanation.surface: A small argument is escalating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blowing up' suggests a row exploding but is a light wind rising.
explanation.definitionFit: Old slang for a squabble shares its spelling with a gentle wind.

clue.text: Original calling ?

parts.note: calling read as what one is called, and original as first, so the clue asks for a first name rather than a first career

explanation.surface: Someone wonders what their first vocation was.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Calling' suggests a vocation, but here it is the name one is called by, the one that comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: A Christian or given name comes before the surname, so it is the first of one's names.

clue.text: An upper -class -sounding way to restart

indicators.note: sounding says the words are judged by how they are said, not spelt

parts.note: U is the old label for upper-class usage, so An plus U

explanation.surface: A posh-voiced method of beginning again.
explanation.walkthrough: U and non-U were Nancy Mitford's labels for upper- and lower-class British speech.
explanation.definitionFit: To begin afresh is to start over again.

clue.text: Swimmer appears to be in difficulties

definitions.meaning: a flatfish found in coastal waters

explanation.surface: A bather looks to be struggling in the water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'appears to' is a link joining the two meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: A flatfish is a sea creature that swims; to struggle clumsily is to be in trouble.

clue.text: What, confusion ended this period of -the world's history!

definitions.text: What, confusion ended this period of -the world's history!

parts.words: What, confusion ended this period of -the world's history!
parts.note: the clue asks for a long cold era of the planet's past whose ending, by thaw and melt, it pretends was a muddle

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims in surprise that chaos brought an era to a close.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is a whimsical cryptic definition of the long glacial era of prehistory; the exact joke behind 'confusion' is uncertain.
explanation.definitionFit: A glacial epoch is a long stretch of geological time when ice sheets covered much of the land.

clue.text: She's not the pick of the bunch

definitions.text: She's not the pick of the bunch

parts.words: She's not the pick of the bunch
parts.note: a woman left unchosen at a dance, punning on a garden bloom not picked for a bouquet

explanation.surface: A girl is overlooked in favour of others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pick of the bunch' plays on flowers picked for a bouquet and on dancers chosen as partners.
explanation.definitionFit: A shy person left sitting out at a dance shares a name with a garden flower that grows by walls.
